tribe: Khath'am of Yemen — Banu Malik ibn Quhafa
teaser: She sailed to Abyssinia, married Ja'far, then Abu Bakr, then Ali — and Umar brought his dreams to her.

layers.title: Who She Was
layers.subtitle: Not Quraysh, and it never held her back
layers.content:
Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage at full length, and the length is the point: Asma bint Umays ibn Ma'add ibn Taym ibn al-Harith ibn Ka'b ibn Malik ibn Quhafa, and on through nine more names to Aftal, who is Khath'am.

Khath'am was a Yemeni tribe. She was not Quraysh, not Ansar, not a client of any Makkan house. In a city where a woman's standing came from her father's clan, she had no clan in Makkah at all.

Her sisters mattered as much as her father. One of them, Salma bint Umays, married Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib and bore him a daughter, Umamah. Ibn Sa'd mentions this in passing while listing Hamza's children, and it turns out later to decide something.

Asma herself married Ja'far ibn Abi Talib — the Prophet's ﷺ cousin, the brother of Ali, a man of Banu Hashim. A Yemeni woman with no Makkan tribe married into the house of the Prophet ﷺ himself.

One more thing worth noting before the story moves. She appears in Vol. III not only as somebody's wife but as somebody's authority. When the second caliph of Islam wanted a dream interpreted, he went to her, and the report of it is in his own words.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the entries on Abu Bakr as-Siddiq and Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: Onto a ship, out of Arabia, for years
layers.content:
The sources place her among the early Muslims of Makkah without pinning a date on it. What they do fix is where she went.

When the persecution made Makkah unliveable, a group of Muslims crossed the Red Sea to Abyssinia and put themselves under the protection of a Christian king. Asma and Ja'far were among them. Ibn Sa'd's Vol. III fixes the length of it almost by accident: while arguing that Ja'far could not have been paired in the brotherhood of Madinah, al-Waqidi observes that Ja'far had emigrated to Abyssinia before that and came back seven years later.

Seven years. Read it slowly. She left the sanctuary of her own peninsula, learned to live in a foreign court, and bore children who had never seen Makkah or Madinah. While the Muslims of Madinah were building a mosque, fighting Badr and Uhud, and receiving revelation week by week, she was on the other side of a sea, hearing about it late or not at all.

That is a particular kind of cost, and it is the one least often described. Nobody beat her. She simply lost the years.

al-Mubarakpuri records the end of it: the Prophet ﷺ wrote to the Negus asking him to send Ja'far and his companions home, and they came back to him at Khaybar.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III (al-Waqidi's note on Ja'far's years in Abyssinia); al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the letter to the Negus

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: Two migrations, and a custody case she decided by existing
layers.content:
Sahih Muslim preserves an exchange from soon after the return, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who had been on the ship with them.

Asma was visiting Hafsah when Umar came in. Told who she was, he said that they, the Muhajirun to Madinah, had a better claim to the Prophet ﷺ than she did. She did not let it stand. You were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, she said, and he fed your hungry and taught your ignorant, while we were in the land of the distant and the hated, and that was for Allah and His Messenger. She went to the Prophet ﷺ and repeated it. He answered that no one had a better claim than she did: Umar and his companions have one migration, and you, the people of the ship, have two.

Vol. III records a second thing, small on the page and large in what it says. Hamza's orphaned daughter Umamah needed a guardian, and Ali, Ja'far and Zayd ibn Haritha each wanted her. The Prophet ﷺ gave custody to Ja'far, and Ibn Sa'd states the reason plainly: because the girl's maternal aunt, Asma bint Umays, was married to him.

A ruling from the Prophet ﷺ turned on which household this woman happened to be in.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions — narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari: 'You have two migrations' (not carried in Ibn Sa'd Vol. III)
layers.source: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the custody of Umamah bint Hamza

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: Widowed at Mu'tah, and again in the caliph's house
layers.content:
In Jumada al-Ula of 8 AH, three thousand Muslims met a Byzantine force many times their size at Mu'tah. Zayd ibn Haritha fell first. Ja'far took the banner, dismounted, killed his own horse so he could not retreat, and fought until his right hand was cut away, then his left, then held the banner with both arms until he was struck in two. al-Bukhari's report counts fifty wounds on his body and not one of them on his back.

Asma was in Madinah with his small sons. She heard it as a widow hears it.

Then Abu Bakr married her, and she bore him a son, Muhammad, born on the road at Dhu al-Hulayfa during the Farewell Hajj of 10 AH. Two years later she was widowed again, and Ibn Sa'd devotes a whole cluster of chains to what happened next: Abu Bakr left instructions that his wife Asma bint Umays should wash his body.

One of those chains carries a detail that no forger would bother with. He told her to do it on a day she was not fasting, because that would give her more strength. She was fasting anyway. At the end of the day she remembered his oath, called for water and drank, and said: by Allah, I will let the breaking of an oath follow him today.

She later married Ali ibn Abi Talib and bore Yahya and Awn.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, on the fifty wounds found on Ja'far's body at Mu'tah — cited by al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
layers.source: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Battle of Mu'tah; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the washing of Abu Bakr, and the children of Ali

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: The woman the second caliph asked about a dream
layers.content:
Near the end of his life Umar ibn al-Khattab stood on the minbar on a Friday and told the people he had dreamt of a red cock pecking him twice, and that he took it to mean his term was near. Then he named his source. I recounted it to Asma bint Umays, he said, and she told me that a Persian man would kill me.

He was killed by Abu Lu'lu'ah, a Persian, in the mosque.

Ibn Sa'd also lists her in the first register of state stipends, among the earliest of the Muhajirun women: Asma bint Umays a thousand dirhams, Asma bint Abi Bakr a thousand, the mother of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud a thousand.

What the ummah kept from Asma bint Umays, may Allah be pleased with her, is a shape rather than a saying. Trace her ties and you cross the whole first generation: sister to Hamza's wife, aunt and then guardian's wife to Hamza's orphan, wife of the martyr of Mu'tah, wife of the first caliph and the woman who washed his body, wife of the fourth, mother of Abdullah ibn Ja'far and of Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr. Households that would later be set against each other in history books all ran through one Yemeni woman who had no clan in Makkah at all.

She held them together by being in them.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — Umar's dream and his register of stipends

quiz.prompt: Where did Asma bint Umays spend the years of her first marriage?

options.text: In Ta'if, under the protection of Thaqif
In Abyssinia, under the protection of the Negus
In Yemen with her own tribe
In Madinah with the Ansar

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III (al-Waqidi's note that Ja'far came back seven years later); al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ eventually wrote to the Negus asking for them, and they reached him at Khaybar. She had been out of Arabia for years while the community's decisive events happened without her.

quiz.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ tell her when Umar said the Muhajirun of Madinah had a better claim to him?

options.text: That Umar was right and she should not argue
That she and the people of the ship had two migrations, not one
That claims of precedence were forbidden
That her reward would come only in the Garden

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions — narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
quiz.scholar_reflection: Abu Musa, who had been on the ship himself, transmits it. She went and asked directly rather than absorbing the slight, and the answer became a permanent point of honour for a whole group of Muslims.

quiz.prompt: Why did the Prophet ﷺ give custody of Hamza's orphaned daughter Umamah to Ja'far?

options.text: Because Ja'far was the eldest of the three claimants
Because Hamza had asked for it before Uhud
Because the girl's maternal aunt, Asma bint Umays, was married to him
Because Ali and Zayd withdrew their claims

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the entry on Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ali, Ja'far and Zayd ibn Haritha all wanted the child. The deciding factor named in the report is Asma's presence in the house, through her sister Salma bint Umays, Umamah's mother.

quiz.prompt: What did Abu Bakr instruct concerning his own body when he was dying?

options.text: That Umar should wash him
That his wife Asma bint Umays should wash him
That he be buried unwashed as a martyr
That Aishah should wash him

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — multiple chains on the washing of Abu Bakr
quiz.scholar_reflection: He added that she should do it on a day she was not fasting, so she would have the strength. She was fasting; she broke it deliberately at the end of that day and said she would let the breaking of an oath follow him.

quiz.prompt: Whom did Umar ibn al-Khattab name from the minbar as the one who interpreted his dream of the red cock?

options.text: Ka'b al-Ahbar
Aishah bint Abi Bakr
Asma bint Umays
Ubayy ibn Ka'b

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — Umar's Friday address on his dream
quiz.scholar_reflection: She told him a Persian man would kill him. He said it publicly, and he was killed in the mosque by a Persian shortly afterwards.

quiz.prompt: Her hardest years cost her nothing dramatic — only distance and time while the important things happened elsewhere. Have you had a season like that?

options.text: Yes, and I am still catching up on what I missed
Yes, and it turned out to be the making of me
I have always managed to be where things were happening
I am in one now and cannot yet tell which it is

quiz.citation: Reflection on the years in Abyssinia — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Nobody beat her and nobody starved her. She lost seven years of proximity, which is a loss with no scar to show for it.

quiz.prompt: When her precedence was dismissed to her face, she stated her case and then took it higher. What do you do when your effort is not counted?
quiz.slider_label: Speaking up for your own worth

options.text: Say nothing and let the record correct itself
State the facts plainly, once, and leave it there
Take it to someone who can settle it
Nurse it privately, which I know is the worst option

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
quiz.scholar_reflection: Her reply was not a complaint about feelings. It was an account of facts: where they had been, what it had been for. Then she asked the one person entitled to rule on it.

quiz.prompt: She was widowed twice and married three times, and every household she entered she carried something into. What do you bring into a new room of people?

options.text: Memory — I keep the previous people alive in the new place
A clean start, deliberately
Skills and usefulness more than history
Caution, until I know the ground

quiz.citation: Reflection on the marriages of Asma bint Umays — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Her sons by three fathers grew up as brothers. Whatever she carried between those houses, it was strong enough to hold across two funerals.

quiz.prompt: Abu Bakr asked her to wash his body and she broke her fast because of an oath he had made. Whose small instructions do you take that seriously?

options.text: One or two people, and I would notice every detail
I keep the spirit of what people ask, not the letter
I am better at big promises than small ones
Honestly, I forget most of what people ask of me

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the chains on the washing of Abu Bakr
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had told her to do it on a non-fasting day for her own sake. She was fasting, did the work anyway, and then settled his words by drinking at the end of the day.

quiz.prompt: A caliph brought his dream to a woman from a tribe with no standing in Makkah. Whose judgement do you actually seek, and does it match whose you should?

options.text: The people with titles, if I am honest
The quiet person who has seen more than they say
Whoever will agree with me
I mostly decide alone and then look for confirmation

quiz.citation: Reflection on Umar's Friday address concerning his dream — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Umar had the whole of Madinah to consult. He named her from the minbar, which means he was not embarrassed to have asked her.
